content.text: By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
State the conditions needed for iron to rust
Distinguish between rusting and other forms of corrosion
is a specific type of corrosion that affects iron and steel. It causes billions of pounds of damage worldwide each year. Understanding how rust forms allows us to prevent it.
is the corrosion of iron. It is an oxidation reaction.
- iron will not rust if either is absent.
Does not protect the iron underneath (unlike aluminium oxide)
Continues to spread into the metal
Iron(II) ions are further oxidised to iron(III)
Iron(III) ions react with hydroxide ions and water to form rust
Greatly increases rate (salt water conducts better)
[DIAGRAM: Four test tubes with iron nails in different conditions: (A) air and water, (B) boiled water with oil layer (no oxygen), (C) dry air with desiccant (no water), (D) salty water]
Both water AND oxygen are needed for rusting. Salt speeds it up.
1. Barrier Methods (keep out water and oxygen)
If the barrier is scratched, rusting can occur underneath.
A more reactive metal is attached to the iron. The reactive metal corrodes instead of the iron.
Zinc is more reactive than iron
Even if scratched, the zinc still protects the iron
Used for: roofing, car bodies, fencing, buckets
These electrons prevent iron from losing its electrons
Iron remains protected even if coating is damaged
Blocks of zinc or magnesium attached to iron structures
Used on: ships, oil rigs, underground pipes
Must be replaced periodically as they corrode away
[DIAGRAM: Ship's hull showing sacrificial zinc blocks attached below waterline]
Iron alloyed with chromium (and often nickel)
Chromium forms a protective oxide layer
Used for: cutlery, surgical instruments, kitchen sinks
This layer is tough and protective
An iron nail is placed in a test tube containing boiled water covered with a layer of oil. Explain why the nail does not rust.
Boiling removes dissolved oxygen from the water
The oil layer prevents oxygen from the air entering
Both water AND oxygen are needed for rusting
Explain how galvanising protects iron from rusting.
Galvanising coats iron with a layer of zinc
Zinc is more reactive than iron
If the coating is scratched, zinc reacts preferentially
Zinc loses electrons instead of iron: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻
These electrons protect the iron from oxidation
Why does rusting occur faster near the sea?
Salt water is a better conductor than pure water
This allows electrons to transfer more easily
The electrochemical reactions of rusting happen faster
More exposure to water spray also increases rusting
BOTH water AND oxygen are needed
Only iron and steel rust; other metals corrode differently
Thinking tin plating uses sacrificial protection
Tin is a barrier method; tin is LESS reactive than iron
State the two substances that must be present for iron to rust. (2 marks)
Describe an experiment to show that both water and oxygen are needed for rusting. (6 marks)
Explain why salt water causes iron to rust faster than pure water. (3 marks)
Explain how galvanising protects iron from rusting, even if the zinc coating is scratched. (4 marks)
Compare painting and galvanising as methods of rust prevention. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of each. (4 marks)
A ship has blocks of zinc attached to its hull below the waterline.
a) Explain why this prevents the hull from rusting. (3 marks)
b) Why must the zinc blocks be replaced periodically? (2 marks)
The corrosion of iron by reaction with oxygen and water
The gradual destruction of a metal by chemical reaction
Coating iron with zinc for protection
Using a more reactive metal to protect iron from corrosion
Preventing rusting by coating iron to exclude air and water
An alloy of iron with chromium that resists corrosion
Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃·xH₂O
Salt, acid, and heat speed up rusting
painting, oiling, plastic coating, tin plating
works even if scratched (zinc corrodes instead)
